title: Descriptions in 105 CMR 720.010 and the appendix to 105 CMR 720.000 that differ from the current M.G.L. c. 112, § 12D, 105 CMR 721.020(B) and M.G.L. c. 17, § 13(a)
subtopic: Older descriptions of the prescription form and the commission
rule_summary: 105 CMR 720.010 states that 105 CMR 720.000 establishes the list of interchangeable drug products from which a pharmacist must interchange a reasonably available less expensive drug product than that written, when a prescription written by a practitioner indicates 'interchange'. The Foreword printed in Appendix A at 105 CMR 720.200 states that the Drug Formulary Commission is comprised of nine men and women appointed by the Governor, that M.G.L. c. 112, § 12D mandates prescription forms that allow practitioners to prescribe interchangeable drug products by simply signing the signature line, and that a practitioner who determines that a brand name drug product should be dispensed must sign the signature line and write the words 'no substitution' in his or her own handwriting in the space provided below the signature line. The Introduction in the same appendix states that § 12D mandates prescription forms with one signature line; that if the prescriber signs the prescription form and writes 'no substitution' in his or her own handwriting in the space provided below the signature line, the pharmacist must fill the prescription exactly as indicated; and that if the prescriber signs and does not write 'no substitution' under the signature, the pharmacist is legally required to dispense a less expensive, equivalent interchangeable drug product listed in the Massachusetts List of Interchangeable Drugs if one is reasonably available. The current text of M.G.L. c. 112, § 12D provides that every prescription issued in the commonwealth by a practitioner shall meet the Department's standards for format; that the standards shall require that the indication of 'no substitution' not be the default indication and that the prescription indicate 'Interchange is mandated unless the practitioner indicates "no substitution" in accordance with the law'; and that, except in cases where the practitioner has indicated 'no substitution', the pharmacist shall dispense an interchangeable abuse deterrent product if one exists or, if none exists, a less expensive, reasonably available, interchangeable drug product as allowed by the most current formulary or supplement thereof. The Department's standard in 105 CMR 721.020(B) requires that the indication of 'no substitution' not be the default indication, that the Prescription carry that statement, and that the indication be a unique element in the Prescription not satisfied by use of any other element, including the signature. Neither M.G.L. c. 112, § 12D nor 105 CMR 721.020(B) states a handwriting requirement. M.G.L. c. 17, § 13(a) provides for a drug formulary commission consisting of 16 members.
exam_relevance: Tests that a candidate who reads 105 CMR 720.010 or the Foreword and Introduction in its appendix still applies the current M.G.L. c. 112, § 12D and 105 CMR 721.020(B), under which interchange is mandated unless 'no substitution' is indicated as a unique, non-default element that the signature does not satisfy, with no handwriting requirement, and an interchangeable abuse deterrent product comes first where one exists; and that M.G.L. c. 17, § 13(a) provides for a commission of 16 members.

common_confusions: Requiring 'no substitution' to be handwritten below the signature line, as the Foreword and Introduction in the appendix describe. The current § 12D and 105 CMR 721.020(B) require a non-default, unique indication that the signature does not satisfy and state no handwriting requirement.

Reading 105 CMR 720.010 as making interchange depend on a prescription that indicates 'interchange'. Under the current § 12D interchange is mandated unless the practitioner indicates 'no substitution'.
Taking the size of the drug formulary commission from the Foreword's nine members. M.G.L. c. 17, § 13(a) provides for 16.
